source.title: Choose What to Manipulate: Revealing Data Scaling Laws in Bounding-Box Guided Policies for Semantic Manipulation
source.authors: Yi-Hao Wu; Jin-Ming Ma; Jun-Bo Tan; Yan-Zhao Yu; Shoujie Li; Ming-Liang Zhou; Di-Yun Xiang; Xue-Qian Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor formatting/OCR artifacts, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how robotic-policy generalization scales with the number of bounding-box objects and finds diminishing, saturating returns; it compares power-law fits with alternatives and says the power law is only approximate over the tested range.
record.gate_note: The scaling experiment concerns robotic manipulation performance versus bounding-box object diversity, not language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute. Rows cover its directly measured scaling results and curve fits. The policy-baseline comparisons, detection-corruption tests, and cross-task success rates do not measure the scaling versions and are not included.
record.test_reason: The study fits scaling curves for real-robot manipulation scores (optimality gap = 1 − normalized score) against the number of bounding-box object classes (1–16). No version names this. There is no held-out loss, and model parameters, tokens and compute are not varied. The measure is a task score against data diversity in imitation learning. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say all four fitted models agree on a monotonic but diminishing trend. They argue their bounded formulation fits better than Lin et al.'s unbounded power law. They add that more object diversity reduces the demonstrations needed per object.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies bounding-box object diversity for real-world robotic policies and fits models to generalization optimality gap; it does not reproduce language-model loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling curve and preferred fit are evaluated separately for Rubbish Disposal and Drink Fetching; the power-law fit is only described as approximate over the tested range of one to sixteen objects.

fits_no_version.finding: In real-robot bounding-box-guided diffusion policies, the optimality gap falls monotonically with object-class count (1–16) with diminishing returns. Exponential (R² 0.994/0.999) and saturating fits beat a power law (R² 0.944/0.992) by AIC on both tasks. Power-law exponents are −0.76 and −0.72, and the authors call the power law only approximate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robot imitation-learning generalization scales with training-object diversity in a bounded, saturating way rather than as an unbounded power law.

record.problems: The scaling study covers two robotic tasks and a tested object-count range of one to sixteen; the text says the power-law description is approximate over that range. Numerical data points for the scaling curves are presented in figures rather than tabulated.
record.rows_left_out: Per-configuration normalized-score points in Fig. 7 and per-object details are not numerically tabulated in the text, so they were not separately extracted. The study says it compares candidate fits using BIC, but no BIC values appear in the provided Table III.

untested.parts: All: no language-model loss, and no parameter, token or compute scaling.
All: no extrapolation to larger runs.
No loss scaling with params, tokens or compute in any modality. The study scales task score with object diversity only.
No comparison of fitting choices for LM loss laws or compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Power-law AIC values (−23.9 Rubbish Disposal, −32.6 Drink Fetching) are not recorded although the other models' AIC values are.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'challenges' and V7 'supports' labels are dropped. The construct is task score vs object diversity in robotics, not loss vs params, tokens or compute. The saturation partly follows from the bounded score: the score cannot exceed 100%.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between language-model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of language-model architecture details such as depth and width at fixed parameter count.

Tests robotic-policy performance against bounding-box object count, not loss scaling in image/video models or the effects of repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer generally; does not vary parameters, tokens, or compute.
Downstream language-model performance scaling or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Does not study language-model parameter-counting, schedules, data choices, compute-optimal splits, or disagreements among language-model scaling-law studies.
